questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 5\text{ kg}$ is pulled along a smooth horizontal surface by a constant pulling force $F = 40\text{ N}$ directed at an angle $\theta = 60^\circ$ above the horizontal. If the block is displaced horizontally by $d = 10\text{ m}$, what is the total work done by the pulling force?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Rigid block on frictionless horizontal plane

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Calculating scalar work via dot product W = F * d * cos(theta).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires resolving vector component and multiplying, not bare recall.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed W = F * d * cos 60° = 40 * 10 * 0.5 = 200 J.

B.diagnostic: Ignored the angle theta and calculated W = F * d = 400 J.

C.diagnostic: Used sin 60° instead of cos 60°, computing perpendicular component instead of along displacement.

D.diagnostic: Incorrectly assumed forces at an angle do zero work.

progressive_hints.title: Definition of Mechanical Work
progressive_hints.text: Work done by a constant force is defined by the dot product $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos \theta$.

progressive_hints.title: Identifying Parameters
progressive_hints.text: Here $F = 40\text{ N}$, $d = 10\text{ m}$, and $\theta = 60^\circ$. Note that $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$.

progressive_hints.title: Calculation
progressive_hints.text: $W = 40 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 200\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: The scalar product for work: $W = F d \cos \theta$.
Substitute values: $W = (40\text{ N})(10\text{ m})\cos 60^\circ = 400 \times 0.5\text{ J} = 200\text{ J}$.

questions.stem: A satellite of mass $m$ orbits the Earth in a uniform circular orbit of radius $R$ with constant orbital speed $v_0$. What is the net work done on the satellite by the gravitational force during one complete orbit of period $T$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Satellite in circular orbit around central Earth

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Identifying that centripetal gravitational force is everywhere orthogonal to velocity vector dr/dt, yielding zero work.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying vector orthogonality or conservation of kinetic energy.

A.diagnostic: Correctly identified that F_g is strictly perpendicular to displacement dl at every instant, so dW = F . dl = 0.

B.diagnostic: Confused the gravitational potential energy magnitude with the work done during an orbit.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied gravitational force by circumference 2*pi*R ignoring the orthogonality.

D.diagnostic: Equated orbital kinetic energy with work done per orbit.

progressive_hints.title: Direction of Gravitational Force
progressive_hints.text: In a circular orbit, Earth's gravity acts radially inward toward the center.

progressive_hints.title: Direction of Motion
progressive_hints.text: The velocity vector is strictly tangential, perpendicular to the radial direction at every point.

progressive_hints.title: Dot Product Property
progressive_hints.text: Since $\vec{F} \perp d\vec{r}$, $\vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = F ds \cos 90^\circ = 0$. Total work is identically zero.

derivation_steps: Instantaneous work $dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{r}$.
For circular motion, $\vec{F}_g = -\frac{G M m}{R^2}\hat{r}$ and $d\vec{r} = R d\theta \hat{\theta}$.
Since $\hat{r} \cdot \hat{\theta} = 0$, $dW = 0$ at every instant.
Alternatively, by the Work-Energy Theorem, $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m v_0^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_0^2 = 0$.

limiting_cases.condition: Arbitrary closed path in conservative field

questions.stem: Two bodies $A$ and $B$ have masses $m_A = 2\text{ kg}$ and $m_B = 8\text{ kg}$ respectively. If both bodies have the exact same linear momentum magnitude $p$, what is the ratio of their kinetic energies $\frac{K_A}{K_B}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two independent moving particles

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Using relation K = p^2 / (2m) to deduce inverse proportionality to mass at constant momentum.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires algebraic ratio setup, not bare fact retrieval.

A.diagnostic: Correctly applied K = p^2 / (2m) to deduce K_A / K_B = m_B / m_A = 8 / 2 = 4.

B.diagnostic: Inverted the ratio, assuming K is directly proportional to mass at constant p.

C.diagnostic: Assumed equal linear momentum implies equal kinetic energy.

D.diagnostic: Squared the mass ratio (8/2)^2 = 16.

progressive_hints.title: Relation Between Momentum and Kinetic Energy
progressive_hints.text: Linear momentum is $p = mv$ and kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Expressing K in terms of p
progressive_hints.text: Multiply and divide by $m$: $K = \frac{(mv)^2}{2m} = \frac{p^2}{2m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Ratio Evaluation
progressive_hints.text: For constant $p$, $K \propto \frac{1}{m}$, so $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{m_B}{m_A} = \frac{8}{2} = 4$.

derivation_steps: Kinetic energy: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$.
Given $p_A = p_B = p$:
$K_A = \frac{p^2}{2 m_A}$, \quad $K_B = \frac{p^2}{2 m_B}$.
Ratio: $\frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{m_B}{m_A} = \frac{8\text{ kg}}{2\text{ kg}} = 4$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: K_A -> infinity (photons/light particles carry extreme KE per momentum)

questions.stem: An electric water pump lifts $1200\text{ kg}$ of water from a well of depth $h = 15\text{ m}$ in a time of $t = 60\text{ s}$ at constant speed. What is the average power output of the pump? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Water column and pump mechanism
idealizations: Negligible kinetic energy imparted to outflow

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Calculating gravitational work mgh and dividing by time delta t to find average power.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires multi-step numerical calculation mgh/t.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed P_avg = mgh / t = (1200 * 10 * 15) / 60 = 180000 / 60 = 3000 W (3 kW).

B.diagnostic: Reported total work done W = 180000 J without dividing by time t = 60 s.

C.diagnostic: Calculated m * h / t without multiplying by gravitational acceleration g.

D.diagnostic: Divided mass by time (1200/60) and multiplied by height without g.

progressive_hints.title: Work Done Against Gravity
progressive_hints.text: Lifting mass $m$ to height $h$ requires work $W = mgh$.

progressive_hints.title: Definition of Average Power
progressive_hints.text: Average power is the rate of work done: $P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}$.

derivation_steps: Work done lifting water: $W = m g h = (1200\text{ kg})(10\text{ m/s}^2)(15\text{ m}) = 180{,}000\text{ J}$.
Average power: $P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{180{,}000\text{ J}}{60\text{ s}} = 3000\text{ W} = 3\text{ kW}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: P -> 0 (infinitely slow pumping requires zero power)
P -> 0 (zero vertical lift requires zero work against gravity)

questions.stem: A body moves along the $+x$-axis under the action of a variable force $F(x)$ shown in the accompanying graph. The force increases linearly from $0$ to $20\text{ N}$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 4\text{ m}$, and then remains constant at $20\text{ N}$ from $x = 4\text{ m}$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$. What is the total work done by the force as the body moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Particle undergoing 1D constrained displacement

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating work as the area under the F-x curve (triangle + rectangle).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires interpreting graphical F(x) geometric area rather than applying a closed formula.

A.diagnostic: Correctly integrated area under F(x): Triangle Area = 0.5 * 4 * 20 = 40 J; Rectangle Area = (8 - 4) * 20 = 80 J; Total = 120 J.

B.diagnostic: Treated the entire region as a rectangle F_max * x_total = 20 * 8 = 160 J.

C.diagnostic: Only computed the rectangular portion from 4 m to 8 m (80 J), ignoring the first segment.

D.diagnostic: Only computed the triangular portion from 0 to 4 m (40 J).

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Meaning of Work
progressive_hints.text: Work done by a 1D force is the area under the force-displacement graph: $W = \int F(x) dx$.

progressive_hints.title: Splitting the Area
progressive_hints.text: Split the area into a triangle from $x = 0$ to $4\text{ m}$ and a rectangle from $x = 4$ to $8\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Summing Areas
progressive_hints.text: $A_1 = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 20 = 40\text{ J}$, $A_2 = 4 \times 20 = 80\text{ J}$. Total work $W = 40 + 80 = 120\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: Work is defined as $W = \int_0^8 F(x) dx$.
From $x = 0$ to $x = 4\text{ m}$: $F(x) = 5x\text{ N}$. Area $A_1 = \frac{1}{2}(4\text{ m})(20\text{ N}) = 40\text{ J}$.
From $x = 4$ to $x = 8\text{ m}$: $F(x) = 20\text{ N}$. Area $A_2 = (8 - 4\text{ m})(20\text{ N}) = 80\text{ J}$.
Total work: $W = A_1 + A_2 = 40\text{ J} + 80\text{ J} = 120\text{ J}$.

questions.stem: An ideal horizontal spring with spring constant $k = 400\text{ N/m}$ is fixed to a rigid wall. A block of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ is pushed against the spring, compressing it by $x = 0.1\text{ m}$ from its natural equilibrium length. When released from rest on a frictionless horizontal floor, what is the speed of the block as it passes through the equilibrium position ($x = 0$)?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block-spring closed mechanical system

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying conservation of mechanical energy between spring elastic potential and kinetic energy.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires setting up conservation of mechanical energy state equation U_i + K_i = U_f + K_f.

A.diagnostic: Correctly equated 0.5 * k * x^2 = 0.5 * m * v^2 => v = x * sqrt(k/m) = 0.1 * sqrt(400/2) = 0.1 * sqrt(200) = sqrt(2) m/s.

B.diagnostic: Used U = k*x^2 without the 0.5 factor, finding v = x * sqrt(2k/m) = 2.0 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Calculated v = k*x / m = 400 * 0.1 / 2 = 20 m/s then took wrong roots or factors.

D.diagnostic: Forgot square root when solving for v.

progressive_hints.title: Spring Potential Energy
progressive_hints.text: The elastic potential energy stored in an ideal spring compressed by $x$ is $U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Mechanical Energy Conservation
progressive_hints.text: On a frictionless floor, elastic potential energy converts entirely into kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Solving for Speed
progressive_hints.text: $v = x \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = 0.1 \times \sqrt{\frac{400}{2}} = 0.1 \times \sqrt{200} = 0.1 \times 10\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: Mechanical energy at release: $E_i = U_i + K_i = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 + 0$.
Substitute values: $E_i = \frac{1}{2}(400)(0.1)^2 = 200 \times 0.01 = 2\text{ J}$.
At equilibrium ($x = 0$): $E_f = 0 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Conservation: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 2\text{ J} \implies \frac{1}{2}(2)v^2 = 2 \implies v^2 = 2 \implies v = \sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: v -> 0 (infinitely heavy block gains negligible velocity)

questions.topic: Work, Energy and Power: Work-Energy Theorem, Conservative Forces & Power
questions.stem: A car of mass $m$ traveling at speed $v$ skids to a complete stop over a braking distance $s_1$ on a horizontal asphalt road when the driver locks the wheels. If the initial speed is doubled to $2v$ under identical road and tire friction conditions, what will be the new skid distance $s_2$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Car vehicle skidding on horizontal ground

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying the Work-Energy Theorem to deduce quadratic scaling of stopping distance with initial velocity s proportional to v^2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires functional scaling analysis s(v) = v^2 / (2 mu g).

A.diagnostic: Correctly applied W_net = Delta K: -mu_k * m * g * s = -0.5 * m * v^2 => s = v^2 / (2 mu_k g). Doubling v quadruples s.

B.diagnostic: Assumed stopping distance scales linearly with velocity like stopping time t = v / (mu g).

C.diagnostic: Applied square root scaling instead of quadratic scaling.

D.diagnostic: Assumed cubic scaling s proportional to v^3.

progressive_hints.title: Work Done by Friction
progressive_hints.text: The retarding friction force is $f_k = \mu_k m g$. The work done by friction over distance $s$ is $W_f = -f_k s$.

progressive_hints.title: Work-Energy Theorem
progressive_hints.text: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K \implies -\mu_k m g s = 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies s = \frac{v^2}{2\mu_k g}$.

progressive_hints.title: Scaling Ratio
progressive_hints.text: Since $s \propto v^2$, when speed is doubled ($v \to 2v$), distance becomes $(2)^2 s_1 = 4 s_1$.

derivation_steps: Net horizontal force during locked-wheel braking: $F_{\text{net}} = -\mu_k m g$.
Work done by friction: $W = -\mu_k m g s$.
By Work-Energy Theorem: $W = K_f - K_i = 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Equating: $\mu_k m g s = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies s = \frac{v^2}{2\mu_k g}$.
For $v' = 2v$: $s_2 = \frac{(2v)^2}{2\mu_k g} = 4 \left(\frac{v^2}{2\mu_k g}\right) = 4 s_1$.

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: s -> 0 (car already at rest stops immediately)
s -> infinity (frictionless surface never stops the car)

questions.topic: Work, Energy and Power: Work-Energy Theorem, Conservative Forces & Power
questions.stem: A particle moves in 1D along the $x$-axis subject to a conservative force corresponding to potential energy function $U(x) = 5 x^2 - 20 x + 15$, where $x$ is in meters and $U$ is in Joules. What is the value of the force $F(x)$ acting on the particle at position $x = 3\text{ m}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: 1D particle in conservative potential field

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Calculating force as negative spatial gradient of potential energy F = -dU/dx.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires taking derivative and substituting x = 3 m.

A.diagnostic: Correctly differentiated F(x) = -dU/dx = -(10x - 20) = 20 - 10x. At x = 3 m, F = 20 - 30 = -10 N.

B.diagnostic: Forgot the negative sign in F = -dU/dx, computing +dU/dx = 10(3) - 20 = +10 N.

C.diagnostic: Confused the equilibrium point x = 2 m (where F = 0) with x = 3 m.

D.diagnostic: Evaluated -10x without adding the +20 constant term.

progressive_hints.title: Fundamental Relation Between Force and Potential Energy
progressive_hints.text: For a 1D conservative force, $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.

progressive_hints.title: Differentiating U(x)
progressive_hints.text: Given $U(x) = 5x^2 - 20x + 15$, the derivative is $\frac{dU}{dx} = 10x - 20$.

derivation_steps: Definition of conservative force: $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$.
Derivative: $\frac{d}{dx}(5x^2 - 20x + 15) = 10x - 20$.
Force expression: $F(x) = -(10x - 20) = 20 - 10x$.
At $x = 3\text{ m}$: $F(3) = 20 - 10(3) = 20 - 30 = -10\text{ N}$ (directed along $-x$ direction, pulling back toward equilibrium at $x = 2\text{ m}$).

limiting_cases.expected_outcome: F = 0 (stable equilibrium minimum of potential well)
F < 0 (restoring force directed back to equilibrium)

questions.topic: Work, Energy and Power: Work-Energy Theorem, Conservative Forces & Power
questions.stem: An elevator cab of total mass $M = 1000\text{ kg}$ is hoisted upward by a motorized steel cable. Starting from rest, the elevator accelerates uniformly upward at $a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$ for the first $4\text{ s}$. What is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the tension force in the cable at time $t = 3\text{ s}$? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Elevator cab attached to tension cable

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Determining dynamic tension T = M(g+a), instantaneous velocity v(t) = at, and instantaneous power P = T * v.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires coupling Newton's second law dynamic equilibrium with instantaneous power.

B.diagnostic: Ignored the upward acceleration when calculating tension: used T = Mg = 10000 N, giving P = 10000 * 6 = 60 kW.

C.diagnostic: Only computed the net accelerating power (M*a)*v = 2000 * 6 = 12 kW, ignoring the gravitational component.

D.diagnostic: Divided the instantaneous power by 2, confusing it with average power over the interval.

progressive_hints.title: Cable Tension Calculation
progressive_hints.text: By Newton's second law for upward acceleration: $T - Mg = Ma \implies T = M(g + a)$.

progressive_hints.title: Instantaneous Velocity
progressive_hints.text: Starting from rest, velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$ is $v = at = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Instantaneous Power
progressive_hints.text: $P(t) = T \cdot v(t) = 12{,}000\text{ N} \times 6\text{ m/s} = 72{,}000\text{ W} = 72\text{ kW}$.

derivation_steps: Upward equation of motion: $T - Mg = Ma \implies T = M(g + a) = 1000(10 + 2) = 12{,}000\text{ N}$.
Instantaneous speed at $t = 3\text{ s}$: $v(3) = at = (2\text{ m/s}^2)(3\text{ s}) = 6\text{ m/s}$.
Instantaneous power delivered by tension: $P = T v = (12{,}000\text{ N})(6\text{ m/s}) = 72{,}000\text{ W} = 72\text{ kW}$.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum consists of a bob of mass $m$ attached to a light inextensible string of length $L = 2\text{ m}$. The bob is released from rest when the string makes an angle $\theta_0 = 60^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the speed of the bob and the tension in the string as it passes through the lowest vertical point of its swing? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

questions.stem: A block of mass $m = 4\text{ kg}$ slides down a curved track of vertical height $H = 5\text{ m}$. Due to friction along the track, $50\text{ J}$ of mechanical energy is dissipated as thermal energy. With what speed does the block reach the bottom of the track? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Block and curved rough track

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Applying modified work-energy theorem Delta E_mech = W_non-conservative = -E_thermal.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying non-conservative energy partition rather than ideal energy conservation.

A.diagnostic: Correctly applied E_initial = mgh = 4 * 10 * 5 = 200 J; E_final = 200 - 50 = 150 J; 0.5 * 4 * v^2 = 150 => 2 v^2 = 150 => v^2 = 75 => v = sqrt(75) = 5*sqrt(3) m/s.

B.diagnostic: Completely ignored friction dissipation: v = sqrt(2gH) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.

C.diagnostic: Subtracted dissipated energy from velocity directly rather than from total energy.

D.diagnostic: Computed v = sqrt(2 * E_diss / m) = sqrt(25) = 5 m/s.

progressive_hints.title: Initial Mechanical Energy
progressive_hints.text: At height $H = 5\text{ m}$, the initial potential energy is $U_i = mgH = 4 \times 10 \times 5 = 200\text{ J}$, and $K_i = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Balance with Dissipation
progressive_hints.text: The mechanical energy lost to friction is $50\text{ J}$, so the final kinetic energy is $K_f = U_i - E_{\text{diss}} = 200 - 50 = 150\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.title: Solving for Final Speed
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = 150 \implies 2 v^2 = 150 \implies v^2 = 75 \implies v = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s}$.

derivation_steps: By the Work-Energy Theorem in presence of non-conservative forces: $\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = W_{\text{nc}} = -50\text{ J}$.
$E_{\text{mech}, i} = mgH = (4\text{ kg})(10\text{ m/s}^2)(5\text{ m}) = 200\text{ J}$.
$E_{\text{mech}, f} = 200\text{ J} - 50\text{ J} = 150\text{ J} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$.
Solving for $v$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 150}{4}} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ m/s} \approx 8.66\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Substitute and Evaluate

questions.stem: A particle of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ moves in a conservative 1D potential field defined by $U(x) = x^3 - 3x$, where $x$ is in meters and $U$ is in Joules. Which of the following statements correctly identifies the positions and stability classifications of the equilibrium points?

system_parameters.system_boundary: 1D particle moving in cubic potential well

options.A: Stable equilibrium at $x = +1\text{ m}$, Unstable equilibrium at $x = -1\text{ m}$
options.B: Stable equilibrium at $x = -1\text{ m}$, Unstable equilibrium at $x = +1\text{ m}$
options.C: Both $x = +1\text{ m}$ and $x = -1\text{ m}$ are stable equilibria

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Finding extrema via dU/dx = 0 and determining stability via the sign of d^2U/dx^2.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires second-derivative curvature analysis of potential energy function.

A.diagnostic: Correctly determined dU/dx = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 => x = +-1. d^2U/dx^2 = 6x: at x = +1, curvature > 0 (stable well); at x = -1, curvature < 0 (unstable hill).

B.diagnostic: Inverted the curvature condition, confusing potential maximum with stable equilibrium.

C.diagnostic: Assumed all stationary points where force is zero are stable equilibria.

D.diagnostic: Assumed the origin x = 0 is an equilibrium point, but dU/dx(0) = -3 != 0.

progressive_hints.title: Equilibrium Condition
progressive_hints.text: Equilibrium occurs where force is zero: $F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$.

progressive_hints.title: Finding Critical Points
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{dU}{dx} = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 0 \implies x = +1\text{ m}$ or $x = -1\text{ m}$.

progressive_hints.title: Second Derivative Stability Test
progressive_hints.text: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 6x$. At $x = +1$, $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = +6 > 0$ (local minimum = stable). At $x = -1$, $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = -6 < 0$ (local maximum = unstable).

derivation_steps: Force is zero at equilibrium: $F = -\frac{dU}{dx} = -(3x^2 - 3) = 0 \implies x = \pm 1\text{ m}$.
Stability is determined by the sign of $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2}$ (potential curvature):
At $x = +1\text{ m}$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = 6 > 0$. The potential is concave upward (well), meaning any displacement produces a restoring force back to $x = 1$. This is STABLE equilibrium.
At $x = -1\text{ m}$: $\frac{d^2U}{dx^2} = -6 < 0$. The potential is concave downward (crest), meaning displacement produces a destabilizing force away from $x = -1$. This is UNSTABLE equilibrium.

questions.stem: A box of mass $m = 10\text{ kg}$ is gently placed with zero initial horizontal velocity onto a long horizontal conveyor belt moving at a constant speed $v = 6\text{ m/s}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the belt is $\mu_k = 0.3$. What is the work done by kinetic friction on the box during the slipping phase until it moves synchronously with the belt? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)

system_parameters.system_boundary: Box placed on continuous moving belt
idealizations: Constant conveyor speed maintained by motor

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating the positive work done by kinetic friction in the ground frame W_f = +0.5 m v^2 = +180 J.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires resolving the authentic misconception that friction work is universally negative.

A.diagnostic: Correctly recognized that friction accelerates the box in the direction of motion in the lab frame, doing positive work W_f = Delta K_box = +0.5 * 10 * 6^2 = +180 J.

B.diagnostic: Dogmatically claimed friction work must always be negative, ignoring that it accelerates the box.

C.diagnostic: Computed the work done by the belt motor W_motor = m * v^2 = 360 J instead of the work on the box.

D.diagnostic: Claimed zero work because the box eventually comes to relative rest on the belt.

progressive_hints.title: Direction of Friction on the Box
progressive_hints.text: Relative to the belt, the box slips backward. Therefore, the belt exerts a forward kinetic friction force on the box in the direction of belt motion.

progressive_hints.title: Work-Energy Theorem in Ground Frame
progressive_hints.text: The box starts from rest ($v_i = 0$) and reaches speed $v = 6\text{ m/s}$. The only horizontal force acting on the box is kinetic friction.

progressive_hints.title: Evaluating Work on the Box
progressive_hints.text: $W_{\text{friction, on box}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2 - 0 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(6^2) = +180\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: Forward friction force on box: $f_k = \mu_k m g = 0.3 \times 10 \times 10 = 30\text{ N}$.
Acceleration of box: $a = \frac{f_k}{m} = \mu_k g = 3\text{ m/s}^2$.
Time to reach synchronous speed $v = 6\text{ m/s}$: $t = \frac{v}{a} = \frac{6}{3} = 2\text{ s}$.
Displacement of box in ground frame: $s_{\text{box}} = \frac{v^2}{2a} = \frac{36}{2 \times 3} = 6\text{ m}$.
Work done by friction on box: $W = f_k \cdot s_{\text{box}} = 30\text{ N} \times 6\text{ m} = +180\text{ J}$.

Note: The belt moves distance $s_{\text{belt}} = v t = 6 \times 2 = 12\text{ m}$. Work done by belt motor is $f_k \cdot s_{\text{belt}} = 30 \times 12 = 360\text{ J}$. Exactly half ($180\text{ J}$) becomes kinetic energy of the box, and half ($180\text{ J}$) is dissipated as thermal friction.

When cruising at a steady speed of $v_1 = 180\text{ km/h}$, the train's locomotive engine delivers a power output of $P_1 = 2000\text{ kW}$. What power output $P_2$ must the engine deliver to cruise steadily at double the speed, $v_2 = 360\text{ km/h}$?

system_parameters.system_boundary: High-speed streamlined train cruising at terminal velocity
idealizations: Pure aerodynamic drag dominance at high speed

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Deducing cubic scaling of aerodynamic cruising power P = F * v = c * v^3.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying non-linear functional power law scaling P proportional to v^3.

A.diagnostic: Correctly derived P = F * v = (c * v^2) * v = c * v^3. When speed doubles (v -> 2v), power increases by factor 2^3 = 8: P_2 = 8 * 2000 = 16000 kW.

B.diagnostic: Assumed quadratic scaling P proportional to v^2, calculating 4 * 2000 = 8000 kW.

C.diagnostic: Assumed linear scaling P proportional to v, calculating 2 * 2000 = 4000 kW.

D.diagnostic: Assumed fourth-power scaling 2^4 = 16, calculating 32000 kW.

progressive_hints.title: Steady Cruising Equilibrium
progressive_hints.text: At steady speed, the forward engine traction force equals the drag force: $F = F_{\text{drag}} = c v^2$.

progressive_hints.title: Instantaneous Power Relation
progressive_hints.text: Power delivered is $P = F \cdot v = (c v^2) \cdot v = c v^3$. Power scales with the cube of speed!

derivation_steps: At steady cruising velocity: $a = 0 \implies F_{\text{engine}} = F_{\text{drag}} = c v^2$.
Mechanical power is the rate of work done: $P = F \cdot v = (c v^2) v = c v^3$.
Therefore, cruising power exhibits cubic velocity dependence: $P \propto v^3$.
Ratio of powers for $v_2 / v_1 = 2$: $\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^3 = 2^3 = 8$.

questions.stem: A block of mass $m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$ moving at velocity $v_1 = 8\text{ m/s}$ along a smooth horizontal surface collides head-on and elastically with a stationary block of mass $m_2 = 5\text{ kg}$. What is the maximum elastic potential energy stored in the interface during the collision at the instant of maximum deformation?

system_parameters.system_boundary: Two-body colliding system in 1D
system_parameters.reference_frame: Inertial ground frame and Center-of-Mass frame

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesizing center of mass kinetic energy partition: U_max = 0.5 * mu * v_rel^2 where mu = m1*m2 / (m1+m2).

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires decomposing system kinetic energy into CM and relative frames.

A.diagnostic: Correctly computed reduced mass mu = (3*5)/(3+5) = 15/8 kg; U_max = 0.5 * mu * v_rel^2 = 0.5 * (15/8) * 64 = 0.5 * 15 * 8 = 60 J.

B.diagnostic: Assumed the entire initial kinetic energy K_i = 0.5 * 3 * 64 = 96 J converts into potential energy, violating momentum conservation.

C.diagnostic: Calculated CM kinetic energy K_cm = 36 J instead of internal deformation energy.

D.diagnostic: Used simple average of masses in reduced mass formula.

progressive_hints.title: State at Maximum Deformation
progressive_hints.text: At the instant of maximum compression, both blocks have the exact same instantaneous velocity, which is the center-of-mass velocity $v_{\text{cm}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Energy Partition
progressive_hints.text: Total energy is conserved: $U_{\text{max}} = K_{\text{initial}} - K_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}m_1 v_1^2 - \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)v_{\text{cm}}^2 = 96 - \frac{1}{2}(8)(9) = 96 - 36 = 60\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: Initial total kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2}m_1 v_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(8^2) = 96\text{ J}$.
Center-of-mass velocity: $v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 v_1}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{3 \times 8}{8} = 3\text{ m/s}$.

At maximum deformation, relative velocity is zero; kinetic energy of the system is purely the bulk motion of the center of mass: $K_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) v_{\text{cm}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(8)(3^2) = 36\text{ J}$.
By conservation of mechanical energy: $U_{\text{max}} = K_i - K_{\text{cm}} = 96\text{ J} - 36\text{ J} = 60\text{ J}$.
Equivalently, using reduced mass $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{15}{8}\text{ kg}$:
$U_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{15}{8}\right)(8^2) = \frac{1}{2}(15)(8) = 60\text{ J}$.

progressive_hints.text: At the highest point of the loop, gravity pulls downward toward the center. The string tension must satisfy $T_{\text{top}} \ge 0$ for the string to stay taut.

progressive_hints.title: Critical Velocity at Apex
progressive_hints.text: At the apex: $T + mg = \frac{m v_{\text{top}}^2}{L}$. Setting $T \ge 0$ gives $v_{\text{top}}^2 \ge g L$.

For the string not to slacken: $T_{\text{top}} \ge 0 \implies \frac{m v_{\text{top}}^2}{L} \ge mg \implies v_{\text{top}}^2 \ge g L$.
Conservation of mechanical energy between bottom and top points:
$\frac{1}{2}m u^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v_{\text{top}}^2 + mg(2L)$.
Substitute minimum top velocity $v_{\text{top}}^2 = gL$:
$u^2 = gL + 4gL = 5gL \implies u_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{5gL}$.

What is the work done by this force on the particle as it moves along the parabolic path $y = x^2$ from the origin $(0,0)$ to the point $(2,4)$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Evaluating path independence by checking conservative exact differential d(x^2 y) = 2xy dx + x^2 dy.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires identifying conservative nature of vector field via curl F = 0.

A.diagnostic: Correctly observed that F = grad(U) where U = x^2 * y is an exact differential: d(x^2 * y) = 2xy dx + x^2 dy. Therefore W = U(2,4) - U(0,0) = (2^2)(4) - 0 = 16 J.

B.diagnostic: Integrated each component independently without accounting for cross-differential structure.

C.diagnostic: Divided the potential evaluation by 2.

D.diagnostic: Arithmetical error in evaluating limits.

progressive_hints.title: Check for Conservative Force
progressive_hints.text: Check if $\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}$: $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) = 2x$, and $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2) = 2x$. The force is strictly conservative!

progressive_hints.title: Finding the Scalar Potential Function
progressive_hints.text: Notice that $d(x^2 y) = 2xy dx + x^2 dy$. Thus $\vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = d(x^2 y)$.

progressive_hints.title: Path Independence
progressive_hints.text: The work depends only on initial and final coordinates: $W = \left[ x^2 y \right]_{(0,0)}^{(2,4)} = (2)^2 (4) - 0 = 16\text{ J}$.

derivation_steps: Evaluate work line integral: $W = \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_C (2xy dx + x^2 dy)$.
Verify if the differential form is exact: $\frac{\partial (2xy)}{\partial y} = 2x$, $\frac{\partial (x^2)}{\partial x} = 2x$.
Since mixed partials match, the field is conservative and has scalar potential $V(x,y) = x^2 y$ such that $\vec{F} = \nabla V$.
By the fundamental theorem of line integrals: $W = V(2,4) - V(0,0) = (2^2)(4) - (0^2)(0) = 16 - 0 = 16\text{ J}$.
Independent check along given path $y = x^2, dy = 2x dx$:
$W = \int_0^2 \left[ 2x(x^2) dx + x^2 (2x dx) \right] = \int_0^2 4x^3 dx = \left[ x^4 \right]_0^2 = 2^4 = 16\text{ J}$.
